q: Explain what Nizza DOCG is and how it reordered Barbera d'Asti's hierarchy.
accept: the top subzone of barbera d'asti promoted to its own docg in 2014
nizza is 100 percent barbera from 18 communes around nizza monferrato
nizza docg from 2014 with eighteen months aging six of them in wood
barbera d'asti's best subzone made a separate denomination
ans: Nizza was the best subzone of Barbera d'Asti and in 2014 it was cut loose as a DOCG in its own right, first appearing with the 2014 vintage. It is 100% Barbera, where the parent Barbera d'Asti DOCG allows up to 10% of other varieties, and it comes from 18 communes on the hills around Nizza Monferrato, from lower-yielding, better-exposed hillside sites rather than valley floor. Aging is at least 18 months with a minimum of six in wood, and 30 months with twelve in wood for the Riserva. Below it, Barbera d'Asti keeps its two tiers, the base wine and Superiore at 14 months with six in wood, and Barbera del Monferrato covers wider, humbler ground. The significance is that Barbera, historically the everyday wine the family drank while the Nebbiolo was sold, now has a formal apex — the culmination of a rehabilitation that began with Giacomo Bologna's Bricco dell'Uccellone in 1982, when barrique aging first showed that Barbera's acid could carry oak and age.
exp: Piedmont questions default to Nebbiolo, and a candidate who can speak about Barbera with the same precision stands out. Two traps to avoid: Barbera d'Alba and Barbera d'Asti are different denominations, not a quality ladder, and Nizza is a place, not a style term. The wider lesson is Italy's habit of promoting a subzone out of its parent — Dogliani made exactly the same move out of Dolcetto di Dogliani.

q: Compare Trentodoc and Franciacorta: origins, grapes and aging minima.
accept: trentodoc is alpine and leaner while franciacorta is warmer and broader
trento doc from 1993 with fifteen months on lees against franciacorta's eighteen
ferrari from 1902 in trentino versus franciacorta docg 1995 by lake iseo
trentodoc alpine metodo classico franciacorta on morainic hills in lombardy
ans: Trento DOC, created in 1993, was Italy's first denomination written specifically for metodo classico, but the tradition starts with Giulio Ferrari, who studied in Champagne and brought Chardonnay to alpine Trentino in 1902. The permitted grapes are Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Meunier and Pinot Bianco; minimum lees aging is 15 months for non-vintage, 24 for millesimato and 36 for riserva. The vineyards climb the mountain slopes of the Adige and Cembra valleys to considerable altitude, so the wines are taut, high in acid and slower to ripen. Franciacorta, DOC in 1967 and DOCG since 1995, sits on morainic hills beside Lake Iseo in Lombardy — warmer, lower and lake-moderated, so the wines are broader and riper. Chardonnay, Pinot Nero and Pinot Bianco, with the late-ripening native Erbamat admitted in 2017 to claw back acidity as the climate warms; minimum 18 months on lees and 25 from harvest for non-vintage, 24 on lees for Saten and Rose, 30 for millesimato and 60 for riserva. In short: Franciacorta is longer-aged, richer and better marketed, Trentodoc leaner, more alpine and dominated by one great house, Ferrari.
exp: The examiner is checking that a candidate does not treat Italian metodo classico as one thing. The numbers are the easy half; the causal half is altitude versus lake moderation, which explains why Franciacorta needs Erbamat and Trentodoc does not. Keep Alta Langa in reserve as the third — Piedmont's metodo classico DOCG, vintage-dated by rule, minimum 30 months on lees — and remember that Prosecco's tank method sits outside this conversation entirely.
